extracted.intended_audience: researchers, librarians, prospective authors/readers and editors concerned with academic book-series quality
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the scholarly quality, editorial standards, and integrity of an academic monograph/book series (here: African theological studies). Focuses on peer review, source use, attribution, language, and bibliographic accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review (series claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the title pages of each volume, the series is peer-reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The title-page statement of peer review is presented as a quality marker for the series; readers and evaluators may expect volumes to have undergone external scholarly review. The presence of the claim should be corroborated by editorial practice and quality checks (see editorial oversight criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of African theological characteristics and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The editors of the series seek to promote "the characteristics of African theology and its independence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series scope and stated aims (e.g., emphasising African theological perspectives and independence) are criteria for selecting works and judging thematic fit; many authors being African (mostly Nigerian) is cited as aligned with this aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title-content correspondence (avoid misleading titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Book titles should accurately reflect the content; misleading titles harm the series' editorial integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Edmund Hogan criticises Blaise Okpanachi's volume, noting that although the title purports to study Nigerian–Vatican diplomatic relations for 1884–1950, only twenty-nine pages are relevant. Evaluators should check that the bulk of the text matches the book’s stated topic and title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vetted, authoritative secondary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should rely on authoritative, peer-reviewed, and verifiable sources rather than obscure or non-vetted secondary sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism cites Chimaka using a 2005 New Delhi publication not found in German-speaking Europe catalogues, and copying text from a 2010 source. Series editors and reviewers should expect use of sources accessible and authoritative in relevant scholarly contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of plagiarism and correct attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must not copy verbatim from other works without citation; proper attribution is required for all borrowed text and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples: Nwaigwe allegedly copies almost an entire paragraph from Glenn Olsen without credit; passages are lifted verbatim from Gerard Sheehy and a Liberian newsletter without attribution; Lusabe uses text from Makarios Tillyrides without attribution. The rubric implies use of plagiarism checks and strict editorial enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection of source types for doctoral-level research
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctoral-level monographs should cite appropriate academic primary and secondary sources rather than parish handbooks, newsletters, or donor magazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of inappropriate sources cited include a parish handbook for marriage preparation (Archdiocese of Newark), a Liberian newsletter, and World Vision’s donor magazine. Such sources are flagged as unusual or insufficient for doctoral research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient English language proficiency and copyediting
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must demonstrate adequate command of English and the text should be copyedited to remove grammatical and idiomatic errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of poor language provided: phrases such as "before she finally leaved her home", "such theme like sexuality", and "lead to bloody shedding of human beings." These indicate need for linguistic review or rejection/rewriting if author lacks proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and complete bibliographic citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliographies should list correct author names, publication details, page numbers, and avoid ambiguous or incomplete entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: misspelling 'Hillmann' as 'Hillman' and incorrect series/volume info; listing a translator (Austin Flannery) as the author of a Vatican declaration; missing page numbers and URLs; confusing entries like 'Schrijvers, quoted in Stromquist' without full citation. Editors should enforce bibliographic standards and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Series editors are responsible for ensuring overall quality: title-content fit, vetting and verification of sources, checking for plagiarism, ensuring linguistic quality, and correct bibliographies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article links multiple problems (misleading titles, plagiarism, poor sourcing, language errors, bibliography mistakes) to weaknesses in 'general editorship' and suggests stronger editorial processes (review, copyediting, vetting) are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to doctoral research standards when publishing dissertations
rubrics_metrics.description: Monographs derived from doctoral dissertations should meet doctoral-level standards for sources, originality, attribution, and scholarly rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many series volumes were originally dissertations submitted to the University of Würzburg; the criticism asserts that doctoral theses turned into monographs should not contain unvetted secondary sources, plagiarism, or non-academic citations, and should be subject to rigorous editorial and peer-review scrutiny before publication.
